Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette:
Kai presents as a 75-year-old financial analyst, meticulously dressed and quietly spoken, whose composure seems to be maintained by a visible, constant effort. The precipitating event occurred eight months prior, on a Tuesday evening when they stayed late at the office to finalize a quarterly report. The building was nearly empty when a man they didn't recognize, dressed in a uniform that looked like building security, confronted them in the hallway. He began by criticizing them for working so late, his tone accusatory, implying they were breaking some rule. The criticism escalated, becoming personal and demeaning. "You think you're better than everyone, staying here like this," he'd sneered, backing them into their own office. The assault that followed was brutal and swift, and the man's parting words, a hissed "You know you deserved this," have become a near-constant echo in Kai's mind.

In the months since, Kai has struggled to form a coherent narrative of that night. They describe the memory not as a story but as a collection of jagged, sensory shards. There is the sound of the man's voice, that low, critical tone, which now intrudes at random moments. There is the acrid, metallic taste of blood in their mouth from where they bit their own lip, a taste that can suddenly flood their senses while they are drinking their morning tea or trying to eat lunch, causing them to gag. But they cannot seem to place these fragments in order. The sequence of events feels jumbled and unreliable, a source of profound shame and confusion. This inability to tell a clear story, even to themself, has fostered a terrifying belief: that they cannot rely on their own mind.

This fear permeates every aspect of Kai's life, especially their work. As a financial analyst, their career was built on precision and trust in their own judgment. Now, they are certain they are failing. When their manager recently pointed out a minor calculation error in a report, a routine correction they would have once taken in stride, Kai felt a surge of panic so intense they had to flee to the restroom, convinced this was proof of their complete incompetence. The experience was not just one of professional feedback; it was a visceral echo of the attacker's voice, telling them they were flawed and deserving of punishment. This has made them terrified of any form of criticism, and they have begun avoiding collaborative projects, a withdrawal that has been noted by their colleagues and has strained professional relationships.

The world outside of work has become a landscape of potential threats. The sight of a police car or even a private security guard can trigger a cascade of fear. They find themself scanning crowds, not for any specific danger, but with a generalized sense of dread, a hypervigilance that leaves them exhausted by the end of each day. They have stopped watching the news, as any story of injustice or people in authority misbehaving feels like a personal, physical blow, reaffirming a new, bleak understanding of the world. Before the assault, Kai found meaning in the careful order of their work and the quiet routines of a life lived alone since their spouse's death. Now, that has all evaporated. The meticulous balancing of accounts feels absurd, a pointless exercise in a world where such violence can erupt without reason. Nothing feels meaningful anymore.

Kai's most persistent fear is that these reactions-the fragmented memories, the sensory flashbacks, the overwhelming panic in response to a simple correction-are signs that they are going crazy. The loss of their own internal reliability is the most terrifying consequence of the trauma. They sought therapy after the incident at work, when the shame of their reaction became too much to bear. They fear losing their job, the last structure holding their life together, but more than that, they are desperate to silence the voice and erase the taste, to once again feel that they can trust the workings of their own mind.
